original_summary: Hanamikoji is a two-player card game. Over repeated hands, players use four one-shot actions (Secret, Trade-off, Gift, Competition) to place Item cards beside seven Geisha. Gift and Competition force the opponent to split revealed cards. Winning a majority of a Geisha's Items wins her marker, and the first to 11 Charm or 4 Geisha wins.

review.evidence: No fixed policy works. Always offering your best cards in Gift or Competition hands them to the opponent. Always hoarding by using Secret and Trade-off early leaves forced, transparent Gift and Competition offers late in the hand. Every player must use all four actions each hand, so there is no pass. The seat edge from moving first is removed by alternating the starting player each hand, which over 4 hands gives each seat two starts.

The deal varies, but each player sees 10 of their own cards per hand and controls their timing. Offers can be built so that every split favours the offerer, for example a Competition with two contested-Geisha pairs. A careless player loses Geisha systematically. The previous playtest found the rules sound; luck in the deal is spread over several hands.

Players can improve by sequencing actions, by tracking the 21-card composition to infer the opponent's hand and secret card, and by valuing Geisha differently by Charm and current marker. Ties keep markers, so marker holdings carry over between hands. A weak player still wins Geisha through the opponent's forced offers.

Hands, the secret card, the removed card and Trade-off discards are hidden. Picking from a Gift or Competition means inferring what the offerer is keeping back and what their secret card is likely to be. Making an offer means modelling which split the opponent will take.
Majority counts per Geisha, markers, Charm sums and the 11-Charm or 4-Geisha thresholds are all arithmetic.

The game is turn-based, text-only, has no board and is decided by arithmetic. The previous variation exceeded the limits: about 21 or more attributes against 20, and about 25–30 flat steps against 20. It also left the hand order for the illegal-choice fallback unspecified. The game fits only when the state is packed into list attributes and the end-of-hand work is folded into one calculation.

problems: Attribute count exceeded the limit: 14 per-Geisha count attributes and 7 marker attributes, plus action flags, hand and turn numbers, Charm and Geisha held, the deck, hands, secrets and pile, came to well over 20 while 19 was declared.
Steps per round exceeded the limit: the start-of-hand, turn and end-of-hand steps, with a separate conditional update per Geisha comparison, totalled roughly 25–30 against a declared 15.
Hidden elements were not listed explicitly, so it was unclear that they fit within 3.
Hand order for the illegal-choice fallback was unspecified, so 'the first cards of their hand' was ambiguous.
The declared complexity block was not credible.

changes.what: State is packed into 17 named attributes. Each player's placed counts are one 7-entry list. All seven markers are one 7-entry list. Each player's unused actions are one list. Charm held and Geisha held for both players are one 4-entry 'standing' list. One 'offer' list, one 'chosen action' and one 'pick' hold the current turn.
changes.why: This replaces 14 count attributes and 7 marker attributes with 3, and keeps every tracked number within 20.

changes.what: Start-of-hand work is two conditioned steps: one shuffle, then one update that sets aside, deals, builds the deck and resets actions and counts. End-of-hand work is one step that adds the secrets, one calculation that compares the two count lists, updates the marker list and computes the standing list, one announcement, and one winner step that holds the win check and the hand-4 tiebreak. The fallback and the placement each become one step.
changes.why: This brings the flat step list to 17 per round with 2 choice steps.
changes.fixes: Steps per round exceeded the limit.

changes.what: The rules name exactly three hidden elements. (1) The hidden pile: the deck order plus the out-of-play pile, which holds the removed card and Trade-off cards. (2) The two private hands. (3) The two secret cards.
changes.why: This makes the information structure explicit and verifiably within 3.
changes.fixes: Hidden elements were not listed explicitly.

changes.what: Hand order is defined. Dealt cards are kept in deal order, each drawn card is added at the end, and removing cards keeps the order of the rest. The fallback uses the first cards in this order. The rules also show that a legal fallback always exists, because hand size always covers the remaining actions.
changes.why: This removes the ambiguity in the illegal-choice rule.
changes.fixes: Hand order for the illegal-choice fallback was unspecified.

changes.what: The complexity block is restated from an explicit count of steps and attributes, both listed in the rules.
changes.why: This makes the declared numbers match the build.
changes.fixes: The declared complexity block was not credible.

keeps: Seven Geisha with Charm values 2,2,2,3,3,4,5 and 21 matching Item cards.
The four one-shot actions per hand: Secret, Trade-off, Gift (opponent takes 1 of 3) and Competition (opponent takes 1 of 2 pairs).
One card removed unseen each hand, 6-card hands and an 8-card deck with one draw per turn.
Majority per Geisha wins her marker, ties leave the marker where it is, and markers carry over between hands.
The win at 11 Charm or 4 Geisha, with Charm taking precedence.
The alternating starting player, and all the gameplay rules that the previous test found complete and sound.

recommendation.reason: The game is strategically rich and its rules were found complete. Only the build footprint was over the limits, and packing the state into lists plus one end-of-hand calculation brings it within them without changing play.

variation.name: Hanamikoji: Compact Build
variation.summary: Two players fight over seven Geisha across up to 4 hands of 8 alternating turns. They use four one-shot actions to place, hide, discard or offer Item cards. Gift and Competition force the opponent to split revealed cards. Majorities win Geisha markers, and the first to 11 Charm or 4 Geisha wins.
variation.rules:
COMPONENTS
- Seven Geisha, G1 to G7. Charm values: G1=2, G2=2, G3=2, G4=3, G5=3, G6=4, G7=5 (21 in total).
- 21 Item cards. Each Geisha has as many Items as her Charm value: two G1, two G2, two G3, three G4, three G5, four G6, five G7. A card is named by its Geisha (for example 'G6').
- Each player has four action types: Secret, Trade-off, Gift, Competition.

TRACKED STATE (17 attributes)
1. deck: ordered list of cards, hidden.
2. pile: the out-of-play list, hidden from everyone forever.
3. hand_A: Player A's ordered hand, seen only by A.
4. hand_B: Player B's ordered hand, seen only by B.
5. secret_A: seen only by A until the end of the hand.
6. secret_B: seen only by B until the end of the hand.
7. counts_A: 7 numbers, A's placed cards per Geisha.
8. counts_B: 7 numbers, B's placed cards per Geisha.
9. markers: 7 entries, each 'A', 'N' or 'B'. All start 'N'.
10. actions_A: A's unused actions this hand.
11. actions_B: B's unused actions this hand.
12. hand_number: 1 to 4.
13. turn_number: 1 to 8 within the hand.
14. standing: [Charm held by A, Charm held by B, Geisha held by A, Geisha held by B], all starting 0.
15. chosen_action.
16. offer: the cards revealed this turn, in order, split into Pair 1 and Pair 2 for Competition.
17. pick.

HIDDEN ELEMENTS (3)
(1) The hidden pile: the deck order plus the out-of-play pile, which holds the removed card and all Trade-off cards.
(2) The private hands.
(3) The secret cards.

STRUCTURE
- One engine round is one turn. A hand has 8 turns, and the game lasts at most 4 hands, so at most 32 rounds.
- Active player: in hands 1 and 3, Player A acts on odd turns and B on even turns. In hands 2 and 4, Player B acts on odd turns and A on even turns.

HAND ORDER
- Cards dealt to a hand keep the order they were dealt in.
- A drawn card goes to the end of the hand.
- When cards leave a hand, the remaining cards keep their order.

STEPS OF EACH ROUND
1. (Turn 1 only) Shuffle all 21 Items.
2. (Turn 1 only) The first card goes to the pile. Cards 2–7 go to the first player's hand and cards 8–13 to the second player's hand, where the first player is the one who acts on turn 1. Cards 14–21 form the deck in that order. Both action lists are reset to all four actions. Both count lists are reset to seven zeros. Both secrets are emptied. Markers and standing are NOT reset.
3. The active player moves the first card of the deck to the end of their hand.
4. Show both players: the markers, both count lists, both unused-action lists, the standing, the hand number and the turn number. Each player privately sees their own hand and their own secret.
5. CHOICE: the active player names one unused action and the cards for it:
   - Secret: 1 card.
   - Trade-off: 2 cards.
   - Gift: 3 cards.
   - Competition: 4 cards, the first two being Pair 1 and the last two Pair 2.
6. FALLBACK: the choice is illegal if it names a spent action, a card not held (counting duplicates), or the wrong number of cards. In that case the engine uses the active player's first unused action in the order Secret, Trade-off, Gift, Competition, filled with the first cards of their hand in hand order. A legal fallback always exists, because a player's hand always holds at least as many cards as their remaining actions need: 7 cards against at most 4 needed on their first turn, and exactly the number needed on their last.
7. The chosen cards leave the hand:
   - Secret: the card becomes the active player's secret.
   - Trade-off: both cards go face-down to the pile.
   - Gift or Competition: the cards go to the offer.
8. (Gift or Competition only) The offer is revealed to both players.
9. (Gift or Competition only) CHOICE: the opponent picks. For Gift they pick card 1, 2 or 3 of the offer. For Competition they pick Pair 1 or Pair 2.
10. (Gift or Competition only) An invalid pick becomes option 1.
11. Placement:
   - Gift: the picked card adds 1 to the opponent's count for its Geisha, and the other two cards add 1 each to the active player's counts.
   - Competition: the picked pair adds to the opponent's counts and the other pair to the active player's counts.
   Placed cards are public.
12. The used action is removed from the active player's action list. The offer, chosen action and pick are cleared. The turn number goes up by 1.
13. (After turn 8 only) Both secrets are revealed, each adds 1 to its owner's count for its Geisha, and both secrets are emptied.
14. (After turn 8 only) One calculation, for each Geisha i from 1 to 7:
   - if counts_A[i] > counts_B[i], markers[i] becomes 'A';
   - if counts_B[i] > counts_A[i], markers[i] becomes 'B';
   - otherwise markers[i] is unchanged.
   Then standing is set to [sum of Charm of the 'A' markers, sum of Charm of the 'B' markers, number of 'A' markers, number of 'B' markers].
15. (After turn 8 only) Announce the markers and the standing.
16. (After turn 8 only) Winner check:
   - A player with 11 or more Charm wins. Only one player can, since the total Charm is 21.
   - Otherwise, a player with 4 or more Geisha wins. Only one player can.
   - Otherwise, if this was hand 4, the game ends: higher Charm wins, then more Geisha, else a draw.
17. (After turn 8 only, if the game has not ended) The hand number goes up by 1 and the turn number is set back to 1. The next hand's first player is the other player.

INFORMATION
- Public: placed cards and counts, revealed offers, picks, markers, standing, and spent actions.
- Private: each hand, and each secret until the end of the hand.
- Never revealed: the pile.
- Players may use the known 21-card composition to deduce unseen cards.
variation.objective: At the end of each hand, a player whose markers total 11 or more Charm wins. Otherwise, a player holding 4 or more Geisha markers wins. If neither has happened after hand 4, higher Charm held wins, then more Geisha held, and if both are equal the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Play is unchanged from the previously tested version, which was strategically sound: players sequence their four actions, build offers whose every split favours them, and infer hidden secrets and hands from the 21-card composition. The changes only make the game buildable within 17 attributes, 17 steps, 2 choice steps, 3 hidden elements and 1 random draw per round, and they remove the fallback ambiguity. There are two players, so there is no talk phase.

balanced.evidence:
Item and hand arithmetic checks out. There are 2+2+2+3+3+4+5 = 21 Items, and 1 removed + 6 + 6 + 8 deck = 21. Each player holds 6 + 4 draws = 10 cards and spends 1+2+3+4 = 10, so every action is always fillable. The deck's 8 cards cover the 8 draws.

Win rule. Total Charm is 21, so at most one player reaches 11. Seven Geisha means at most one player reaches 4. The 11-Charm check comes first, matching the original. Example: A holds G4, G6, G7 (12 Charm, 3 Geisha) while B holds G1, G2, G3, G5 (9 Charm, 4 Geisha); A wins. Draws are possible because markers can stay Neutral.

Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule:
(a) Always the lowest unused action (Secret, Trade-off, Gift, Competition) with the first cards in hand. Card selection is effectively random, and the policy never builds majorities. A sensible opponent wins most Geisha: it takes the best card from each Gift and the best pair from each Competition, and plans its own Secret and Trade-off.
(b) Always the last action first (Competition on turn 1). It reveals 4 of only 7 cards with no information. The opponent takes the stronger pair and keeps its own flexibility. This loses to sensible play.
(c) As responder, always pick option 1 (first card or Pair 1). A sensible opponent puts junk first, e.g. Pair 1 = G1+G2 and Pair 2 = G7+G7. Each Competition then nets the policy-holder 2 placements in the weakest Geisha. It loses.
(d) Random play is beaten by sensible play for the same reasons.
No policy never loses, and no action is dominant, because all four must be used each hand.

Seats. A starts hands 1 and 3, B starts hands 2 and 4. The responder-last edge (seeing more before the final action) alternates. A slight asymmetry remains when the game ends after hand 3, since A started 2 of 3 hands, but it is not decisive. Both players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
The rules themselves are complete. Hand order for the illegal-choice fallback is unspecified, which is a minor gap. The game is finite (at most 32 rounds, within 40) and is decided by arithmetic. Two players, so no talk is needed.

The declared complexity is not credible.

Attributes: the rules say the game keeps placed counts per player per Geisha (2×7 = 14) and 7 markers. That is already 21, over the limit of 20, before adding:
- unused actions for 2 players (up to 8 flags or 2 lists),
- the hand number,
- the turn number,
- Charm held and Geisha held for each player,
- the deck, the 2 hands, the 2 secret cards and the out-of-play pile.
The stated 19 is an undercount.

Steps per round: every round's flat step list must contain the conditioned start-of-hand, turn and end-of-hand steps.
- Start of hand: shuffle, remove 1, deal ×2, reset tokens, reset 14 counts. That is at least 5 steps.
- Turn: draw, show state, active choice, Gift resolution, Competition resolution, placement into counts, spend token. That is about 7 steps.
- End of hand: reveal both secrets and add them to counts, compare 7 Geisha and move markers, compute Charm and Geisha held for both players, win check, hand-4 tiebreak. Each Geisha compare is a separate conditional update, and the engine has no lookup or attribute-compare operand, so this needs extra calc steps. That is well over 10 steps.
The total is roughly 25–30 steps, over 20, against a declared 15.

Hidden elements: hands, secret cards, deck order, removed card and Trade-off pile. These are 3 only if grouped generously.

As specified, the design exceeds the attribute and step limits.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
The deal adds variance, and one Item is removed per hand, so luck is not zero. However, the core decisions are skill-driven:
- which cards to Secret or Trade-off,
- how to split Gift and Competition offers so the opponent's best pick still helps you,
- deducing the opponent's hand from the known 21-card composition, the revealed cards and the spent actions,
- targeting high-Charm Geisha toward 11 against the 4-Geisha threat across hands, since markers persist.

Under mutual good play, outcomes depend on how well each player splits and reads offers, not on the deal alone. A strong deal is offset by the opponent choosing first from your Gifts and Competitions. Up to 4 hands with alternating starts average out single-hand luck. Estimated chance share is about 25–35%. A careful reasoner clearly beats a careless one, as the losses of policy (c) show.

required_changes: Cut attributes to 20 or fewer. Store each player's placed counts as one list attribute indexed G1–G7 (2 attributes instead of 14). Store all 7 markers as one list (1 attribute instead of 7). Store each player's unused actions as one list. Then recount honestly, including hand number, turn number, Charm held and Geisha held.

Cut the per-round flat step list to 20 or fewer, counting every `when`-conditioned step. Do the end-of-hand work in a single calc step that compares the two count lists, updates the marker list, and computes Charm and Geisha held for both players. Fold the win check and the hand-4 tiebreak into one conditional winner step. Merge the start-of-hand reset into one step that resets the count lists and token lists.

Restate the complexity block accurately (steps_per_round, attributes, hidden_elements). List the hidden elements explicitly: deck plus removed or Trade-off pile, the two hands, and the two secret cards. Show that they fit within 3.
Define hand order for the illegal-choice fallback, e.g. cards kept in the order dealt or drawn.

balanced.evidence: ARITHMETIC: Charm 2+2+2+3+3+4+5 = 21, and Items per Geisha equal Charm, so there are 21 cards. Per hand: 1 card to the pile, 6+6 dealt, 8 in the deck. Each player draws 4 (one per own turn), so each holds 10 cards in total. Each uses 1+2+3+4 = 10 cards. This is exact. Because total Charm is 21, only one player can reach 11 Charm, and 4 of 7 Geisha is also exclusive, so the winner rule is consistent. The 11-Charm-before-4-Geisha priority matches the original. Example: B holds G1, G2, G3, G4 (4 Geisha, 9 Charm) while A holds G5, G6, G7 (12 Charm), and A wins. MAIN DECISION, Competition with pairs P1/P2. The opponent takes the pair that best improves their margin on contested Geisha. The active player's payoff is the value of the worse pair from their side, so a sensible splitter balances the pairs. Gift: the opponent takes the most valuable single card, so the giver loses its best card. Neither Gift nor Competition is strictly better. Each gives away cards, and their value depends on the current counts and on the hidden hands. Secret (keep 1 hidden) and Trade-off (deny 2) are cheap early but limit later options. No action dominates, because all four must be used exactly once per hand. Only the order and the card choices are decisions. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the WINNER RULE. (a) 'Always first option / pass': this equals the fallback. It plays Secret, Trade-off, Gift, Competition in that order with the first cards in hand order, and as picker always takes option 1. Against a sensible opponent it routinely gives away high-Charm cards (G6, G7) and takes arbitrary picks. The opponent wins G7 and G6 (9 Charm) plus any 2-Charm Geisha, reaching 11, so the policy LOSES most games. (b) 'Always last option' (Competition first, pick Pair 2 / card 3): this is equally blind to card values and loses to sensible play. (c) Against random play each blind policy is roughly a coin flip, not a never-lose outcome. No policy guarantees a win or a draw against every opponent response. Example: if the opponent offers a Competition whose Pair 1 is two G1 and whose Pair 2 is two G7, always picking option 1 hands G7 away. SEATS: the second mover in a hand reacts with more information (the last Competition is chosen against known placements). The first player alternates by hand (A in hands 1 and 3, B in 2 and 4), so over the 4-hand limit each seat leads twice. A game ending early in hand 1 or 3 gives a slight edge to that hand's second player, B. This mirrors the original's accepted near-balance. Both players can realistically win. Markers persist and ties leave markers unchanged, so the game can swing across hands.

playable.evidence: COMPLETENESS: every step names its trigger (turn 1 only / after turn 8 only), its actor and its effect. Deal positions are fixed: card 1 to the pile, 2–7 to the first player, 8–13 to the second, 14–21 to the deck. Hand order rules make the fallback deterministic. Duplicate naming is handled by 'counting duplicates'. Invalid picks become option 1. FALLBACK FEASIBILITY CHECK for any legal order of actions a1..a4: Turn 1: hand 7 ≥ a1 (max 4). Turn 2: hand 8−a1 ≥ a2 since a1+a2 ≤ 7. Turn 3: hand 9−a1−a2 ≥ a3 since a1+a2+a3 ≤ 9. Turn 4: hand 10−(a1+a2+a3) = a4 exactly. So a legal action always exists, as claimed. The deck has 8 cards for 8 draws. The minor wording issue is that step 12 raises turn_number to 9 before the 'after turn 8 only' steps run. Context makes it clear these refer to the round of turn 8, and step 17 resets the number. FINITE: at most 4 hands × 8 turns = 32 rounds. The decision at hand 4 is by Charm, then Geisha count, then a draw, all arithmetic on tracked numbers. LIMITS: 17 steps ≤ 20; 2 choice steps ≤ 4; 17 attributes ≤ 20; 3 hidden elements ≤ 3 (deck and pile grouped as one hidden pile); 1 random draw (shuffle) on turn 1 only ≤ 1; 32 rounds ≤ 40. ENGINE: hidden hands, sequential choice, private values and shared deck draw (workaround via list remove/append) are used. Standing requires a Charm sum over markers, which is a calc and supported. There is no board, no clock, no trading, no binding agreements and no conditional blocks. Per-step 'when' conditions cover the turn-1 and after-turn-8 steps. TALK: this is a 2-player game, so the 3+ talk rule does not apply. Omitting talk is reasonable because the game is about hidden cards, not negotiation. It is not a repeated cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal check is not applicable.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: WHAT DECIDES: the order of actions (when to Secret or Trade-off versus give cards away), how Competition pairs are balanced, which Gift card is taken, and which Geisha to contest given persistent markers. INFERENCE: the 21-card composition is known. Each player can deduce the unseen set: opponent hand + opponent secret + 1 removed card + Trade-off cards, minus all public placements. As the hand proceeds this narrows sharply. Example: after 3 G7 have been placed and you hold 1, the remaining 1 is in the opponent's hand, their secret, the pile, or the deck. This informs Competition splits and picks. Opponent modelling: the opponent's remaining actions are public, so their forced future moves (for example a final Competition of 4 cards) can be anticipated. CHANCE: the deal and the removed card vary hand strength. With 4 hands and persistent markers, I estimate chance decides about 25–35% of results between equal players. EQUAL GOOD PLAY: each hand's split is decided by the deal and by the second-mover position. Over hands, with alternating leads, many games go to hand 3 or 4 and to marker tiebreaks shaped by play choices, not by the shuffle alone. A strong player clearly beats the fallback or a random player. In the original game, skill differences are visible within a few hands.
